chapters.title: The app on my laptop
summary: Today the app lives in your own house: web, api, Postgres and Redis in Docker, plus a one-off migrate job.
Every laptop piece has a twin on AWS. The pencil outlines are the city we will build, chapter by chapter.
On AWS every connection must pass three checks: Reach (roads and guards), Allowed (badges), Password (keys).

chapters.title: AWS basics
summary: We own land (the AWS account) in country us-east-1. The network code selects the first two available availability zones for its districts.
Pulumi, the city planner, builds from our code and keeps a record book (the state) in Pulumi Cloud.
Every building gets name plates (tags), and the treasurer (a $20 budget) emails us before the bill hurts.

chapters.title: The network (VPC)
summary: Our private city minitickets-dev-vpc (10.0.0.0/16): two neighborhoods on the main road, two behind walls.
One city gate (minitickets-dev-igw). The road sign public-rt sends 0.0.0.0/0 to it; private-rt only knows the city.
Public routing comes from the route-table association. No NAT gateway is built: public tasks use assigned public IPs for outbound access; private data subnets have no internet route.

chapters.title: Security groups
summary: The roads exist. Guards now decide which building door accepts which visitor.

ALB reaches web:3000 and API:4000; API reaches DB:5432 and Valkey:6379. Rules reference source groups rather than changing task IPs. SGs are stateful; a route and an allowed port are separate requirements.
A task can have a route and still time out at a closed building door. Compare source SG, destination port and task ENI before blaming the password.

chapters.title: Public IPs and network interfaces
summary: A worker needs an address as well as a guest-list entry.

Fargate awsvpc gives each task an ENI with private address and attached groups. Public-subnet tasks use a public IP for outbound image/secrets access; that does not open inbound ports. Private data has no public entry. No NAT gateway is built.
A public subnet alone does not give a worker internet access. Check route, public-IP assignment and egress; public IPv4 and NAT have different running costs.

chapters.title: The database and cache
summary: Workers need durable records and a shared short-term memory behind the walls.

Postgres is the booking source of truth; Valkey holds sessions, cached event lists, token buckets and advisory inventory. A cache may evict data; SQL transactions and CHECK/unique constraints still protect seats. Data switches and retained backups are independent of compute.

Follow the API ENI to private data subnets. Reach means route + SG, Allowed means the relevant service policy where used, Password means DB/Redis credentials and TLS. Never test by printing secret values.

chapters.title: Secrets
summary: The worker needs a key safe, not passwords written on its name plate.

RDS manages the DB master secret; Valkey/revalidation/origin/signing secrets have distinct purposes and permissions. ECS execution roles inject selected secret fields at task start; application roles fetch only what runtime code needs. Secret ARNs are not secret values.

A task can reach the safe but lack its badge, or have a badge and use the wrong secret field. Rotation needs coordinated credentials and consumer restart/key-ring behavior; automatic ticket key rotation is not built.

chapters.title: ECR
summary: Workers must fetch an immutable packed app from the warehouse.

API, web and worker have separate repositories. Publish builds a git-SHA image once per service, then deployment uses that tag through SSM. Lifecycle policies preserve deployed/recent artifacts; latest is not the release authority. No registry password is committed.
A successful push does not mean a task can pull. Compare image URI/architecture, execution-role ECR permissions and network egress.

chapters.title: ECS
summary: A manager must keep the right packed workers running and replace unhealthy ones.

Fargate arm64 tasks run API and web as separate services; task definitions pin image/env/secrets/roles. Readiness checks data dependencies; liveness only proves a process answers. A dedicated minitickets-dev-migrate task applies SQL before rollout, not inside every API task.
A stopped task has a stoppedReason, exit code and log stream. A service Event often explains image-pull, secret, ENI or health-check failures faster than restarting it.

chapters.title: IAM roles
summary: The manager, workers and publisher need different staff badges.

Trust says who may assume a role; permissions say which actions on which resource ARNs; attachment says which task/function/job uses it. ECS execution roles pull/log/inject secrets; the API task role publishes SNS, queries tickets and signs constrained S3 access; Lambda roles receive their own queue and touch their own outputs.
AccessDenied is not a network timeout. Identify the caller ARN and denied action/resource, inspect trust and permission separately, then check attached taskRoleArn vs executionRoleArn.

chapters.title: The ALB
summary: Visitors need one HTTPS reception desk that sends pages and API calls to healthy staff.

ACM validates minitickets.theversehub.in; HTTPS listener routes /trpc/* to API and other paths to web. Target groups track health independently. ALB-only mode accepts the owner-selected source CIDRs; the committed cdnEnabled=false remains the current shape.
A 502/503 can mean no healthy targets, wrong container port or an application crash. Check listener rule, target health reason, task health and logs in that order.

chapters.title: Service Connect
summary: Web server rendering needs the API without going back through public reception.

Service Connect exposes api/web names via task-local proxies (API proxy 14000, web proxy 13000). API_INTERNAL_URL is server-only; browser requests still use the public /trpc route. Proxy port ingress differs from the application container port.
A browser can work while SSR fails. Check the internal name, Service Connect discovery and proxy SG rule. Localhost-originated internal calls are not trusted for forged X-Forwarded-For.

chapters.title: CloudFront
summary: An optional front layer can bring static files closer to visitors.

CloudFront is implemented but currently inactive: cdnEnabled=false pending account verification. Static assets can be cached; private/RSC/API answers cannot. P10 nonce-bearing HTML is now private,no-store; the events policy min/default TTL 0 honors it. Origin protection uses a secret header and AWS prefix-list mode when enabled.
Do not claim an inactive distribution is live. First diagnose the ALB path; then compare behavior, cache key, origin headers, DNS and certificate region.

chapters.title: CI/CD
summary: A publisher needs a short-lived badge and a deployment record, not laptop keys.

GitHub OIDC trust restricts repository/environment subjects. CI checks code/tests/audit and Trivy images; publish builds SHA artifacts once. Approved deploy prepares the migration task, runs SQL, writes the image tag to SSM, then rolls services/Lambdas. Guards reject stale infrastructure code and superseded approved runs.

An old approved run must not delete newer resources. Distinguish app rollback (old image/current infra) from infra rollback and an additive migration; never locally overwrite the SSM release parameter.

chapters.title: Queues, DLQs and SNS fan-out
summary: Booking commits need two durable consumers without losing messages between SQL and delivery.

The API commits confirmation payload in a Postgres outbox with the booking. A relay publishes to SNS; raw subscriptions copy the event into separate jobs and tickets SQS queues, each with a DLQ/redrive policy. One consumer failure does not block the other.
SNS is fan-out, SQS is durable backlog and retry, the outbox closes the commit/publish gap. A relay can publish twice after an unknown acknowledgement; consumers must be idempotent.

chapters.title: Lambda workers
summary: Queue messages need workers that scale independently from the API.

Email Lambda is 256 MB / 10 s; ticket Lambda is 512 MB / 30 s. Both use the published worker image with different commands. Event-source mappings use partial batch failure responses. They do not need the VPC because their stores are managed AWS APIs, not RDS.

Visibility timeout must outlast processing/retry behavior; partial failure reports only failed message identifiers. Whole-batch failure replays successful siblings; concurrency limits can cause throttling/redrive.

chapters.title: DynamoDB records
summary: Consumers need durable dedupe and owner/date access patterns without an SQL connection pool.

Processed jobs use jobKey plus TTL. Ticket rows use userId/ticketId and by-event-date GSI for a future reminder path. Conditional writes reserve canonical ticket work and support idempotent repair; owner Query is strongly consistent, GSI reads are not. TTL is asynchronous cleanup, not an authorization clock.
Design keys from reads before writing rows. A hot date partition, eventual GSI propagation and duplicate delivery are different failure modes; Query differs from scanning the whole table.

chapters.title: SES delivery
summary: A confirmed booking needs an email delivery service with a verified sender.

SES identity/DKIM records prove sender ownership. Sandbox delivery requires verified recipients and is quota-limited; first AWS delivery remains acceptance work. Lambda IAM restricts sender identities and From address. Provider acceptance is not an exactly-once inbox guarantee.
If SES accepted but the consumer crashed before marking done, retry can send twice. DKIM improves authentication, not universal inbox placement; production access/quota is separate from IAM.

chapters.title: Private S3 assets and signed tickets
summary: A ticket needs a private QR artifact and a short-lived way for its owner to read it.

Bucket ownership/public-access block, SSE-S3 and TLS-only policy protect assets. HMAC signs ticket claims; deterministic seat keys plus conditional Dynamo rows converge under duplicates. API owner-scopes reads and issues 120-second GET/download capabilities. Admin poster PUTs are constrained, staged, byte-checked and copied immutably; CORS is not authorization.
Never log raw signed URLs or signing values. MIME/header checks are not malware scanning/full decoding. Scanner verification/redemption and automated key-ring rotation are explain-only, not shipped.

chapters.title: Alarms and observability
summary: The city diary must show one booking across API and consumers and call for help when backlog grows.

Correlation IDs follow requests, outbox payloads, SNS/SQS and Lambda logs. The four alarm specifications watch the email DLQ, email queue age, worker invocation errors and ALB 5xx. The dashboard includes worker throttles as a metric, not an alarm; ticket DLQ alerting is not built. SNS email subscriptions require confirmation.
An alarm without confirmed email delivery is silent. Missing data policy, evaluation periods and age vs depth matter; search by correlation id before guessing which process failed.

chapters.title: Reminder scheduler (explain-only)
summary: A reminder the day before would branch from ticket date access into the existing email path.

Not built: a daily Scheduler would invoke a reminder Lambda, query tomorrow in by-event-date, and enqueue one email job per ticket/day. No VPC/RDS is needed. The Scheduler badge would trust scheduler.amazonaws.com and allow InvokeFunction on only that function.

Where it would go: a new infra/src/jobs/reminders.ts and apps/worker/src/reminders handler/service beside current workers. Conditional ticket/day dedupe and paginated/sharded date queries prevent duplicate or unbounded sends.

chapters.title: Door check-in (explain-only)
summary: The door would authenticate a QR and atomically consume it once.

Not built: REST API usage plans/API keys throttle staff devices, but are not staff authorization. A check-in Lambda would verify the HMAC then conditionally update valid→used in DynamoDB. Two scans race: one succeeds, one returns already-used time. A staff scanner would keep its key out of the bundle.

Where it would go: apps/web/src/features/checkin plus a check-in Lambda and infra/src/tickets/checkin.ts. HTTP API lacks REST usage-plan features; camera input is untrusted and a signed QR alone is replayable.

chapters.title: Autoscaling (explain-only)
summary: A manager could add workers when traffic grows, but workers cannot create more seats.

Not built: an ECS desired-count target, min 1/max 3, CPU or ALB requests-per-target policy and cost budget. P8 instead builds shared rate limiting and an advisory inventory gate; Postgres still enforces stock. Waiting room, queued booking and expiring customer seat holds are explain-only too.

Where it would go: a new infra/src/compute/autoscaling.ts after services/target groups. More tasks increase DB connections and contention; define a queue-depth/latency objective, cooldown and maximum spend before adding capacity.

chapters.title: Debugging playbook
summary: Follow the failed request through the city rather than restarting unrelated pieces.

Start at the observed symptom and correlation id. Reach checks DNS/routes/SG/ports; Allowed checks IAM caller/action/resource; Password checks secret field/version/TLS without printing values. Then inspect DB locks, pool timeouts, queue age, DLQ/error logs and release SHA.

Change one explanation at a time. A 403 is not fixed by opening a subnet; a lock wait is not fixed by rotating an S3 key. Reproduce in disposable local resources and distinguish local proof from AWS acceptance.

chapters.title: The final poster
summary: The whole city should fit in an explanation you can give without memorizing 100 service names.

Browser→ALB→web/API→Postgres/Valkey is the synchronous path. Booking→outbox→SNS→two SQS queues→Lambdas→SES or S3/DynamoDB is the side path. OIDC/ECR/SSM/CD changes versions. SGs govern reach, IAM grants actions, secrets prove identity. Optional CloudFront and explain-only features remain distinct.
Say which invariant each piece protects and which failure it cannot prevent. Then ask about traffic, latency, durability, privacy and budget before proposing another service.

components.why: QR creation needs recoverable work separate from email, with stable per-seat identity so retries converge on the same tickets.
settings: Same ECR worker image; command ticket-lambda.handler; arm64
Memory 512 MB; timeout 30 s; no VPC attachment
Event source minitickets-dev-tickets; batch 1; maximumConcurrency=2
ReportBatchItemFailures enabled
TICKETS_TABLE, TICKETS_BUCKET and TICKET_SIGNING_SECRET_ID configured; logs /minitickets/dev/tickets

components.debug: If email works while tickets fail, inspect this function rather than the email worker. A creating row can be repaired on retry using its saved token and deterministic object key.
components.interview: Two functions share one release image but select different handlers, roles and queues. Conditional reservation plus deterministic storage makes ticket retries repairable.

components.why: The email consumer needs durable memory of successful work across retries, Lambda instances and later queue redrives.

components.interview: This is completion deduplication keyed by job identity, not a transaction with SES. Sending and marking done have a crash window.

tours.title: Chapter 0: The app on my laptop

steps.title: 1. Locate web container (Next.js)
explain: The Compose web service runs the standalone Next.js image and publishes host port 3100 to container port 3000.
This gives the browser a local production-style UI while server rendering calls the API by its Compose service name.

console.path: Docker Desktop → Containers → minitickets → web → Ports and Logs
console.expect: Profile app; image minitickets-web; 3100:3000; API_INTERNAL_URL=http://api:4000
console.question: How would you explain web container (Next.js) in an interview?

steps.title: 2. Follow api container (Fastify + tRPC)
explain: The Compose API service runs the Fastify/tRPC image on container port 4000 and publishes it on localhost:4100.
Local UI requests need the same server procedures, business rules and datastore queries that the ECS API runs.

console.path: Docker Desktop → Containers → minitickets → api → Ports and Logs
console.expect: Profile app; image minitickets-api; 4100:4000; WEB_ORIGIN=http://localhost:3100
console.question: How would you explain api container (Fastify + tRPC) in an interview?

steps.title: 3. Follow migrate container
explain: The Compose migrate service runs node dist/migrate.js from the API image once, then exits.
Applying SQL before the API starts avoids several API containers racing to change the schema.

console.path: Docker Desktop → Containers → minitickets → migrate → Exit code and Logs
console.expect: Profile app; image minitickets-api; Command node dist/migrate.js; restart=no
console.question: How would you explain migrate container in an interview?

steps.title: 4. Follow postgres container (Postgres 17.6)
explain: The postgres Compose service runs pinned Postgres 17.6 and stores its database files in the postgres_data volume.
Users, event stock, bookings and outbox rows must persist when an API container is replaced.

console.path: Docker Desktop → Containers → minitickets → postgres → Health and Volumes
console.expect: Image postgres:17.6; published port 5432; Volume postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
console.question: How would you explain postgres container (Postgres 17.6) in an interview?

steps.title: 5. Follow redis container (Redis 7.4.5)
explain: The redis Compose service runs Redis 7.4.5 with append-only persistence, a 256 MB memory limit and allkeys-lru eviction.
Local sessions, legacy event-list caching, rate-limit buckets and inventory hints need the Redis protocol used by Valkey in AWS.

console.path: Docker Desktop → Containers → minitickets → redis → Health and Logs
console.expect: Image redis:7.4.5; container port 6379; Host port REDIS_PORT, default 6379
console.question: How would you explain redis container (Redis 7.4.5) in an interview?

steps.title: 1. Locate Your AWS account
explain: The AWS account is the ownership and billing boundary used when Pulumi builds ARNs and restricts role trust policies.
Every deployed resource and temporary credential must belong to the intended account before the network or IAM settings can be trusted.

console.path: AWS account → Account menu → Account ID
console.expect: Local CLI profile ticketlite; Account ID obtained with getCallerIdentityOutput()
console.question: How would you explain Your AWS account in an interview?

steps.title: 2. Follow us-east-1 (N. Virginia)
explain: The committed Pulumi stack selects us-east-1 for regional resources such as the VPC, ECS services, queues and databases.
Keeping the API and its data in one region avoids accidental lookups and deployments against unrelated regional copies.

console.path: AWS console → Region selector → US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1
console.expect: aws:region=us-east-1 in infra/Pulumi.dev.yaml; Console display name US East (N. Virginia)
console.question: How would you explain us-east-1 (N. Virginia) in an interview?

steps.title: 3. Follow First available AZ
explain: The first available zone returned by AWS holds public-1 and private-1 in createNetwork.
The first subnet pair gives the load balancer and managed-data subnet groups one location within us-east-1.

console.expect: Lookup state=available; azNames takes names.slice(0,2); public-1=10.0.0.0/24; private-1=10.0.10.0/24
console.question: How would you explain First available AZ in an interview?

steps.title: 4. Follow Second available AZ
explain: The second available zone returned by AWS holds public-2 and private-2 in createNetwork.
A separate second location satisfies the ALB and data subnet-group shape without placing every subnet in one failure domain.

console.expect: azNames[1] supplies the second zone; public-2=10.0.1.0/24; private-2=10.0.11.0/24
console.question: How would you explain Second available AZ in an interview?

steps.title: 5. Follow Tags: Project, Env, ManagedBy, Name
explain: commonTags sets Project=minitickets, Env=dev and ManagedBy=pulumi; tagsFor(name) adds a resource-specific Name.

console.expect: Project=minitickets; Env=dev
console.question: How would you explain Tags: Project, Env, ManagedBy, Name in an interview?

steps.title: 6. Follow Pulumi stack dev
explain: The dev Pulumi program imports layer functions in infra/index.ts and wires their outputs into dependent resources.
A reviewable TypeScript blueprint records the resource graph and committed environment switches instead of relying on remembered console clicks.

console.question: How would you explain minitickets-dev-monthly-cost in an interview?

console.expect: minitickets-dev-public-2
console.question: Which setting proves this boundary is configured, and which separate boundary could still fail?

steps.title: 4. Follow minitickets-dev-private-2
explain: RDS and ElastiCache ask for subnets in at least two districts, even for a single database.

console.expect: minitickets-dev-private-2

explain: An implicit default network ACL is created with the VPC; the Pulumi program does not add a custom ACL or ACL rules.
The default subnet-edge checkpoint remains relevant when debugging traffic that already passes the project security groups.

console.expect: Default ACL, created by AWS with the VPC; No aws.ec2.NetworkAcl resource in the program
console.question: How would you explain Default network ACL in an interview?

steps.title: 1. Locate minitickets-dev-alb-sg
explain: minitickets-dev-alb-sg is the stateful firewall on the load balancer; its inbound rules select either direct browser access or CloudFront-only origin access.
ALB ingress must match the selected public-entry mode while allowing replies and forwarding to application targets.

console.path: VPC → Security groups → minitickets-dev-alb-sg → Inbound rules and Outbound rules
console.expect: ALB-only mode: TCP 80 and 443 from allowedCidrs, default 0.0.0.0/0; CloudFront mode instead: TCP 80 from com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing
console.question: How would you explain minitickets-dev-alb-sg in an interview?

steps.title: 2. Follow minitickets-dev-web-sg
explain: minitickets-dev-web-sg protects Next.js task network interfaces: ALB traffic enters on TCP 3000, and private API revalidation enters the Service Connect proxy on TCP 13000.
Web tasks should accept page traffic from the ALB and private revalidation through the API Service Connect proxy.

console.path: VPC → Security groups → minitickets-dev-web-sg → Inbound rules and Outbound rules
console.expect: TCP 3000 from minitickets-dev-alb-sg; TCP 13000 from minitickets-dev-api-sg for Service Connect
console.question: How would you explain minitickets-dev-web-sg in an interview?

steps.title: 3. Follow minitickets-dev-api-sg
explain: minitickets-dev-api-sg protects Fastify task network interfaces: ALB traffic enters on TCP 4000, and private web requests enter the Service Connect proxy on TCP 14000. Migration tasks also wear this group.
API tasks should accept public API calls through the ALB and private rendering calls through the web proxy.

console.path: VPC → Security groups → minitickets-dev-api-sg → Inbound rules and Outbound rules
console.expect: TCP 4000 from minitickets-dev-alb-sg; TCP 14000 from minitickets-dev-web-sg for Service Connect
console.question: How would you explain minitickets-dev-api-sg in an interview?

steps.title: 4. Follow minitickets-dev-db-sg
explain: minitickets-dev-db-sg protects the RDS network interfaces with an API-group-only TCP 5432 ingress rule and no outbound rules.
Only task ENIs wearing minitickets-dev-api-sg, including the one-off migration task, should connect to the private SQL database.

console.path: VPC → Security groups → minitickets-dev-db-sg → Inbound rules and Outbound rules
console.expect: TCP 5432 only from minitickets-dev-api-sg; No outbound rules; stateful replies still work
console.question: How would you explain minitickets-dev-db-sg in an interview?

steps.title: 5. Follow minitickets-dev-redis-sg
explain: minitickets-dev-redis-sg protects Valkey network interfaces with an API-group-only TCP 6379 ingress rule and no outbound rules.
Session and cache commands should be reachable only from API tasks that also possess the Redis URL secret.

console.expect: TCP 6379 only from minitickets-dev-api-sg; No outbound rules; stateful replies still work
console.question: How would you explain minitickets-dev-redis-sg in an interview?

steps.title: Redis, revalidation and RDS secrets
